sourceInformation.source: Eye of the Beholder (Westwood Associates / SSI, 1991; MS-DOS and Amiga)
sourceInformation.genre: Real-time, first-person, grid-based party RPG dungeon crawler (a blobber) with lock-and-key puzzles
sourceInformation.perspective: First person at the party's eyes on a 4-way grid, with tweened steps and quarter turns; a top-down parchment automap; full-screen overlay screens over the dimmed 3D view
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.2 (the 2D engine from dist/handoff, patched) and my-3D2dge 3D v0.85.2 (patched), three.js r182 (WebGPU, falling back to WebGL 2) and Rapier 0.19.3 from jsDelivr; AI Hub session client 1.4.0; plain JavaScript bundled into one HTML file; Node 24 and Playwright 1.63.0 (Chromium 1243) for the tests
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's native retro-modern look: code-drawn low-resolution 3D (pixel picture, toon light, outlines, fog, torch shadows), rigs drawn as pixel-art cards, procedural textures, pen-drawn creatures, mechanisms and items, and a brass "lockwork" 10-foot UI with pixel-art item icons
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's procedural rigs and moves (E.Humanoid, E.Blob, E.MOVES and E.Attack wind-ups), a tweened first-person camera (steps, turns, bumps, falls, head bob), pen-animated creatures (leech, rat knot, brass spider, hound, gazer, the Bolt-Holder) and mechanisms (levers, gates, gears, Great Locks, the Undergate's bolts), first-person weapon swings, card and HUD animation
sourceInformation.audio: All code: the engine's chip synth for original step-sequencer songs (title, four floors, boss, camp, ending, race) with fight layers and stings, about 90 synthesized sound effects panned by bearing, and a custom WebAudio formant babble synth for Animalese/Simlish-style voices (one profile per speaker)
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1 in ghost mode, 1 to 4 players: the Rat Run race with the game's own card, other players as cloaked ghosts in their seat colours, progress and a timed result; on its own, a solo Rat Run time trial against your best run's golden ghost
sourceInformation.testing: Any headless testing was allowed. Ran: 22 suites behind one command (tests/run.mjs, printing only failures and a count): lint and reachability of all content, movement, features, items, combat, monsters, magic, camp, progress, save, determinism, babble, art (every monster, person, item and mechanism drawn into a recorder and checked to have its own look and to move), UI flows, Dev Mode, attract mode and a stand-in for the AI Hub in Node, through game.advance and game.debug; a scripted full playthrough by the walkthrough bot on Normal with both of Veil's branches (also run over 20 seeds); Playwright browser checks from file:// on SwiftShader, including a DualSense in standard mapping given to the page through navigator.getGamepads; a suite that reads TASK.md and checks the build against each of its requirements; the AI Hub harness for 2 players, 4 players with latency, jitter and loss, and the host leaving; screenshots at 1280x720 and 1024x768 for the look
sourceInformation.research: The plan's research (Giant Bomb, MobyGames, oldgames.sk on the source; the engine's handoff docs and 3D header; the AI Hub protocol). During the build: reading the engine's docs and source and the hub README; no web research
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux (WSL2); browser unknown (tested in headless Chromium 1243)
sourceInformation.usage: API cost unknown; token counts unknown; session time about 2 hours 45 minutes (18:50 to about 21:35 local, from the clock and file timestamps)

testingFeedback: About 23 real issues: 2 content errors from the lint (decor features facing open floor), 3 bot and balance problems from the full playthrough (a step that never finished, and the party collapsing at the Bolt-Holder in 8 of 20 seeds until the boss and the bot's tactics were tuned; all 20 now win), 1 rest rule (a waiting level-up was lost when a rest ended early), 4 from the browser suite and screenshots (key taps shorter than a frame were dropped, unbound keys did not end the attract mode, a scene crash on null data, the race clock running during its countdown), 6 look and text problems (characters the pixel font lacks, a log over the row labels, a dark parchment, prompts under the dialogue, a title camera inside the party, glare from the Eye), 2 from the AI Hub harness (Enter for Ready was lost while the 3D still loaded; WebGPU errors in the harness's frames, fixed by its WebGL backend) 1 engine warning (the floors ran out of light slots), 1 from checking TASK.md line by line (a key pressed in the attract mode's first 0.3 s was ignored), and 3 from the art suite (four creatures without a walk, strike or idle motion, two scrolls that looked exactly alike, and an empty drawing left unused).

4: the dropped key taps (the party could ignore a quick press at a low frame rate), the lost Ready on the hub's card (the hub would have kept the game out of sessions), the party collapsing at the boss (the campaign could not be finished reliably), and the null-data crash entering play.

The scripted full playthrough: the walkthrough bot plays all four floors and the boss by the real rules in under 2 seconds of test time, so every puzzle, key, ward and deed is proven reachable after each change, and running it over 20 seeds exposed the boss balance.
The engine's own tools/check.mjs: it confirmed there were no errors, but its camera-view cycling and look notes are written for 2D views and found nothing a fixed first-person 3D game could act on.
engineFeedback: Everything drawn by code and deterministic: the 3D engine's pen and THINGS let me build a whole bestiary, every wall mechanism, the boss and 50 item models without one asset file, the 2D rigs drawn as cards gave every person and monster a live, animated look and portrait for free, and the exact fixed step made the whole game testable headless in Node.

Yes, a few times: wall colours come from the legend entry rather than the level's colour, input.hold takes an action not a key code, a scene's data can be null (a default parameter did not catch it), a tap released before the next step reads as pressed but not down, and the 3D worlds run at about 3 frames a second under software rendering, so browser tests had to wait on game state rather than the clock.

The crawler itself as a pure, deterministic sim: the grid party with tweened steps, the formation and per-hand combat, telegraphed monster minds, Vancian magic, camp and food, and a data-driven wiring language for doors, plates, levers, alcoves, teleporters and pits, plus the walkthrough bot that plays it all through the same commands as the player.

Mixing its two UIs and testing the 3D: the engine's pause, settings and save screens are HTML while the game's 10-foot screens are drawn on the canvas, and every check of the 3D look had to run on SwiftShader, slowly.

Two engines, small patches: in the 2D engine, beards and shut eyes for E.Humanoid, PlayStation and Xbox as the only button symbols (PlayStation first), a voice bus with its own volume, panned sound effects, Options ignored while Create is held (the AI Hub rule) and a way to hide Load in a session; in the 3D engine, world.wallBlock, a block made from the level's own wall materials so secret and illusory walls match the walls round them (PATCHES.md lists each).

Let a 3D level's cells change at run time (a wall that opens, a floor that becomes a pit) instead of baking the level once, so secret walls, trapdoors and bridges would not need blocks laid over the baked geometry.
promptFeedback: It is complete and testable: exact deliverables, a detailed plan to build from, clear rules for tests (one command, failures only) and processes, and an exit interview in a fixed shape that the game's About screen can share.

The title rule (brainstorm and pick by a random number) next to a plan that already fixed the title; and whether Online meant the game had to be multiplayer for a genre that is single-player at heart (the plan answered it with a ghost race).

Fitting every system the plan lists (four floors, 16 monster types, 18 spells, camp, NPCs, three input styles, attract mode, Dev Mode, the hub race) into one build and still verifying the 3D look under software rendering.
Say how long a first play of the demo should be and which systems may be cut if time runs short, and allow GPU rendering (or say it is unavailable) for screenshot checks.

aiHub.name: Eye of the Bolt-Holder
aiHub.description: A real-time, first-person party dungeon crawl beneath Hasp, the City of a Thousand Locks: four floors of drains, clockwork halls and eye-cults, levers, plates and keys, spells memorized at camp, and the caged Eye that holds the city's bolts.
aiHub.controls: Stick/WASD move · D-pad/Q E turn · ✕/F use · □/Space strike · L2 R2/1-6 hands · △/I party
